essential: The opening rage of 1862: Adams believes Russell and Palmerston mean to intervene, and the Trent Affair and the escaped cruisers seem to him proof; the Legation lives in unbroken suspense.

After second Bull Run Adams resolves to join the army. His mother is struck more by his pacing over her head; Charles's remonstrance and the duty not to desert his parents hold him back; his father's argument (too late for the campaign; all will go home by spring) decides it.

He returns to copying affidavits from Consul Dudley. Facing friends after defeats is harder than facing enemies, and candor must be affected; include the Times read silently over the muffin and the Cabinet Minister's 'another licking' remark.
London's demonizing of Lincoln and Seward, shown through Thackeray's tearful, ill-founded reproach about Sally Baxter (Mrs. Frank Hampton). Keep the wrong-house comic setup only if it is brief.
Carlyle's jibes heard in silence, and the falling of an idol.
Society is civil but ornamental; Adams holds his tongue.
Diplomats' view of Palmerston: the danger is traps, not lies (Queen's memorandum, Brunnow's 'peau de rhinocere'). Lady Palmerston and Cambridge House succeed inexplicably ('sympathique').
The footman's name-mangling (Handrew, Hanthony, Halexander) and the receiving line with the mechanical laugh.
Minister Adams trusts Russell over Palmerston, while the son sees nothing to choose between them.

The June 1862 Butler woman-order quarrel. Palmerston backs down after the Minister refuses communication except through Russell; this ends the Cambridge House invitations. Adams stays puzzled about why. Keep it as an unresolved question here.

The Fryston visit: Milnes's kindness and the guests Stirling (hatred of Napoleon III), Oliphant (wounded in Japan, arm in sling) and Swinburne (tropical bird). Swinburne's dazzling monologue in Adams's bedroom; Stirling's verdict; Adams's sense that one could only receive.

Adams fails the Hugo and Landor tests, with Milnes's later Hugo anecdote ('un Dieu qui croit en Dieu'). Aftermath: buying 'Queen Rosamund'; the friends drifting apart; Milnes proposing Adams for the St. James's Club, showing he 'was getting on'.
optional: Detailed list of diplomats in the receiving line (Brunnow, Musurus, etc.): reduce to 'the diplomatic corps'.
Moran/Charley Wilson staffing detail in para 3.
Milnes's Yorkshire sanity and hard-drinking Yorkshireman contrast (para 14): condense.
Oliphant's 'Piccadilly'/The Owl aside; Stevenson comparison for Swinburne.
Stubbs household farce and Milnes's 'pretty verses' titles (para 18).
Pickering's seven copies, Moxon and 'Atalanta' penance: may compress to one sentence. Keep the reference to Milnes's female worshipper only if the Hugo anecdote is kept.
Club seconders' names (Tricoupi, Oliphant, Evelyn Ashley): can drop names but keep the 'getting on' irony.
risks: The Fryston section is rich and could crowd out the political first half; keep the weights.

voice_profile: Third-person autobiography in which the old Adams ironically judges young 'Henry Adams' or 'the private secretary'. It moves from concrete scene to aphorism ('a friend in power is a friend lost'), deflates itself constantly ('insect', 'worm', 'small fry'), and builds long periodic sentences out of semicolon series and dashes. It returns to the vocabulary of 'education', 'force', 'unity' and 'chaos'. Irony works through reversal: the lesson learned proves wrong, and the evidence arrives forty years too late. The past perspective of 1862 and the retrospect of the 1900s run side by side and must stay clearly distinguished. Quoted documents, such as letters, despatches and diary entries, serve as evidence that ironizes the narrator's certainties.
